blocks.prompt: 10. Consider the function \(f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \to \mathbb{R}^{+}\) defined by \(f(x) = e^{-x}\). Show that \(f(x)\) is a bijective.
blocks.explanation:
Bijective means one-to-one AND onto, so two things must be checked.
The tool that undoes \(e\) is the natural logarithm: \(\ln(e^t) = t\), \(e^{\ln y} = y\) for \(y > 0\).
Plan: prove one-to-one; test onto for the printed domain \(\mathbb{R}^{+}\); then state when the claim is true.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = e^{-x}\), domain and co-domain \(\mathbb{R}^{+}\) (positive reals).
To find / prove: whether \(f\) is one-to-one and onto.
Method: One-to-one from \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) by taking \(\ln\); onto by solving \(e^{-x} = y\) and checking \(x\) is in the domain.

One-to-one
\[e^{-x_1} = e^{-x_2}\]
\[-x_1 = -x_2 \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2\]
Why: Take \(\ln\) of both sides; \(\ln(e^t) = t\). So \(f\) is one-to-one (on \(\mathbb{R}^{+}\) and on \(\mathbb{R}\)).

Which outputs does \(x > 0\) give?
\[x > 0 \Rightarrow e^{x} > 1\]
\[0 < e^{-x} = \dfrac{1}{e^{x}} < 1\]
Why: \(e^{-x} = \frac{1}{e^x}\), and the reciprocal of a number bigger than 1 lies between 0 and 1. So the range is \((0, 1)\), not all of \(\mathbb{R}^{+}\).

A counter-example to onto
\[e^{-x} = 2 \Rightarrow x = -\ln 2\]
\[-\ln 2 \approx -0.693 \notin \mathbb{R}^{+}\]
Why: \(2 \in \mathbb{R}^{+}\) needs the input \(-\ln 2\), which is negative. So 2 has no pre-image in \(\mathbb{R}^{+}\): as printed, \(f\) is not onto and not bijective.

The true statement: domain \(\mathbb{R}\)
\[y > 0:\; x = -\ln y \in \mathbb{R}\]
\[f(-\ln y) = e^{\ln y} = y \;\checkmark\]
Why: With \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{+}\), every positive \(y\) has the pre-image \(-\ln y\), so \(f\) is onto; with the one-to-one step, \(f\) is bijective.

Check with the graph
Why: Every horizontal line \(y = c\), \(c > 0\), meets the whole curve exactly once (one-to-one and onto \(\mathbb{R}^{+}\)), but for \(c \ge 1\) it meets it at \(x \le 0\), outside the printed domain.
blocks.final_answer: As printed (\(f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \to \mathbb{R}^{+}\)), \(f\) is one-to-one but not onto (range \((0, 1)\)), so it is not bijective. For \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{+}\), \(f(x) = e^{-x}\) is bijective (pre-image of \(y\) is \(-\ln y\)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book asks to show that \(f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \to \mathbb{R}^{+}\), \(f(x) = e^{-x}\), is bijective. As printed this is false: for \(x > 0\), \(e^{-x}\) lies in \((0, 1)\), so for example \(2 \in \mathbb{R}^{+}\) is never an output (even with \(0\) included in \(\mathbb{R}^{+}\) the range is only \((0, 1]\)). The intended statement is \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{+}\), which is bijective (equally true: \(f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \to (0, 1)\)). No answer is printed in the key.
